{{short description|Non-local model for non-linear dispersive waves}}
In [[mathematical physics]], the '''Whitham equation''' is a non-local model for [[non-linear system|non-linear]] [[dispersion relation|dispersive]] [[wave]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Debnath|2005|p=364}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Naumkin|Shishmarev|1994|p=1}}</ref><ref name="Whitham_1974">{{harvtxt|Whitham|1974|pp=476–482}}</ref>

The equation is notated as follows:{{Equation box 1|cellpadding|border|indent=:|equation=<math>   \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t}
  + \alpha \eta \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x}
  + \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} K(x-\xi)\, \frac{\partial \eta(\xi,t)}{\partial \xi}\, \text{d}\xi
  = 0. </math>|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA}}This [[integro-differential equation]] for the oscillatory variable ''η''(''x'',''t'') is named after [[Gerald Whitham]] who introduced it as a model to study [[wave breaking|breaking]] of non-linear dispersive [[water wave]]s in 1967.<ref name="Whitham_1967">{{harvtxt|Whitham|1967}}</ref> Wave breaking – bounded solutions with unbounded [[derivative]]s – for the Whitham equation has recently been proven.<ref name="Vera_2017">{{harvtxt|Hur|2017}}</ref>

For a certain choice of the [[integral kernel|kernel]] ''K''(''x''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''ξ'') it becomes the '''Fornberg–Whitham equation'''.

==Water waves==
Using the [[Fourier transform]] (and its inverse), with respect to the space coordinate ''x'' and in terms of the [[wavenumber]] ''k'':
* For [[surface gravity wave]]s, the [[phase speed]] ''c''(''k'') as a function of wavenumber ''k'' is taken as:<ref name="Whitham_1967"/>

::<math>
  c_\text{ww}(k) = \sqrt{ \frac{g}{k}\, \tanh(kh)},
</math> {{pad|2em}} while {{pad|2em}} <math>\alpha_\text{ww} = \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{\frac{g}{h}},</math>

:with ''g'' the [[Earth's gravity|gravitational acceleration]] and ''h'' the [[average|mean]] water depth. The associated [[integral kernel|kernel]] ''K''<sub>ww</sub>(''s'') is, using the inverse Fourier transform:<ref name="Whitham_1967"/>

::<math>
  K_\text{ww}(s) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} c_\text{ww}(k)\, \text{e}^{iks}\, \text{d}k
                 = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} c_\text{ww}(k)\, \cos(ks)\, \text{d}k,
</math>
:since ''c''<sub>ww</sub> is an [[Even and odd functions|even function]] of the wavenumber ''k''.

* The [[Korteweg–de Vries equation]] (KdV equation) emerges when retaining the first two terms of a [[series expansion]] of ''c''<sub>ww</sub>(''k'') for [[long wave]]s with {{nowrap|''kh'' ≪ 1}}:<ref name="Whitham_1967"/>

::<math> 
  c_\text{kdv}(k) = \sqrt{gh} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{6} k^2 h^2 \right),
</math> {{pad|3em}} <math>
  K_\text{kdv}(s) = \sqrt{gh} \left( \delta(s) + \frac{1}{6} h^2\, \delta^{\prime\prime}(s) \right),
</math> {{pad|3em}} <math>
  \alpha_\text{kdv} = \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{\frac{g}{h}},
</math>

:with ''δ''(''s'') the [[Dirac delta function]].

* [[Bengt Fornberg]] and Gerald Whitham studied the kernel ''K''<sub>fw</sub>(''s'') – [[nondimensionalization|non-dimensionalised]] using ''g'' and ''h'':<ref name="Fornberg_Whitham">{{harvtxt|Fornberg|Whitham|1978}}</ref>

::<math>K_\text{fw}(s) = \frac12 \nu \text{e}^{-\nu |s|}</math> {{pad|2em}} and {{pad|2em}} <math>c_\text{fw} = \frac{\nu^2}{\nu^2+k^2},</math> {{pad|2em}} with {{pad|2em}} <math>\alpha_\text{fw}=\frac32.</math>

:The resulting [[integro-differential equation]] can be reduced to the [[partial differential equation]] known as the '''Fornberg–Whitham equation''':<ref name="Fornberg_Whitham"/>

::<math>
  \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} - \nu^2 \right)
  \left( 
    \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t}
    + \frac32\, \eta\, \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x}
  \right)
  + \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x}
  = 0.
</math>

:This equation is shown to allow for [[peakon]] solutions – as a model for waves of limiting height – as well as the occurrence of wave breaking ([[shock wave]]s, absent in e.g. solutions of the Korteweg–de Vries equation).<ref name="Fornberg_Whitham"/><ref name="Whitham_1974"/>
